chapter.title: The loop: goal, think, act, check, repeat

cards.body:
"Book me a table for 4, Friday at 8" is one sentence. Hand it to an agent and it can turn into several small trips around the same circle.

Your new intern works the same way. They don't disappear and come back with a booking. They **take one step, look at what happened, and decide the next one**, lap after lap, until the job is done.
cards.simpler: "Book me a table for 4, Friday at 8" is one short sentence. Give it to an agent and it may turn into several small trips around the same circle. Think of a new intern. They don't vanish and come back with a booking. They **take one step, look at what happened, and pick the next one**, again and again, until the job is done.

cards.prompt: You leave your intern a sticky note: "Book a table for 4 at Lucia's, Friday 8pm." What do they actually do first?

options.text: Book it in one go and come back saying "done".
Take one small step, like finding Lucia's booking page, then look at what they found.
Write out every step up front and follow them without looking up.

whyNot.a: That mixes up the request with the work. You asked in one sentence, but a booking takes several steps, and each one depends on the last.
whyNot.c: That's a fixed recipe, not a loop: if Friday at 8 is full, step 4 of a plan written in advance is already useless.

cards.reteach: Think about how you'd book it yourself. You search, open the page, see what's free, then choose. Each move depends on what the last one showed you, and an agent works the same way.

cards.title: Four stops on one circle
cards.body:
Most agents run some version of this loop. It starts with a *goal*, the task you gave it. Then the model *thinks*: it reads the goal and picks **one next step**, like "search for Lucia's website".

Next comes *act*. Ordinary software carries out that step, the way the intern actually walks over and picks up the phone. Then comes *check*: whatever came back, a web page or an error, goes to the model.

You'd think the agent writes a full plan and then follows it. Many don't: they decide again on every lap. Some do sketch a plan first, but they still revise it as results come in. That's exactly why an agent can cope when Friday is full.
cards.simpler: Most agents go around some version of this circle. It starts with a goal, the task you gave it. Next, the model thinks and picks **one next step**, like "search for Lucia's website". Then comes act: plain software does that step, like the intern picking up the phone. Last is check: whatever came back, a web page or an error, goes to the model. Many agents don't plan everything first, and the ones that do still change the plan as results come in. Deciding fresh each lap is how it copes when Friday is full.

cards.title: Priya's Friday table
cards.body: Priya asks an agent to book Lucia's for 4, Friday at 8. Lap 1: it searches and finds the booking page. Lap 2: it opens the page and learns 8pm is full, **something no plan written in advance could have known**. Lap 3: it checks 8:30, which is free, but the goal said 8, so lap 4 asks Priya, and she types "fine". Lap 5 books it, a confirmation number comes back, and only then does the model say done: five laps, and Priya's whole part was one word.
cards.simpler: Priya asks an agent to book Lucia's for 4, Friday at 8. Lap 1: it searches and finds the booking page. Lap 2: it opens it and sees 8pm is full, **something no plan made ahead could know**. Lap 3: 8:30 is free, but she said 8. Lap 4: it asks her, and she types "fine". Lap 5: it books, gets a confirmation number, and only then says done. Five laps, and Priya typed one word.

cards.prompt: An agent's goal: find the cheapest train from Leeds to York on Saturday. On lap 2 the ticket site sends back an error: "Service unavailable." What should happen next?

options.text: The error goes back to the model, which picks a new step, like trying a different ticket site.
The agent reports the cheapest fare it found, which is none, and stops.
The software keeps clicking the same button until it works, without telling the model.

whyNot.b: That skips the think stop instead of finishing the job: an error is a result to react to, not an answer to the goal.
whyNot.c: That's act without check: if the model never sees the error, nobody in the loop can choose a smarter next step.

cards.reteach: Every result, good or bad, goes back to the model before the next move. An error is just one more thing the intern brings back to the desk. Then the model decides what to try next.

cards.title: What the model sees each lap
cards.body:
Here's the odd part. On every lap, the model is handed **the whole trail**: the goal, every step it took, every result that came back. Picture the intern rereading a growing stack of sticky notes before each move.

That stack is how a surprise changes the plan. "8pm full" lands on top, and the next step changes.

Researchers led by Shunyu Yao named this pattern *ReAct*: think about the next step, act, then read the result. The loop ends when the model decides the goal is met, or when a limit you set stops it.
cards.simpler: Oddly, each lap the model gets **the whole trail**: the goal, every step, and every result. Picture the intern rereading a growing pile of sticky notes before each move. That pile is how a surprise changes the plan: "8pm full" lands on top, so the next step changes. Researchers led by Shunyu Yao called this ReAct: think, act, read the result. The loop ends when the model says the goal is met, or when your limit stops it.

cards.body: Tom's agent tells him "Table booked for Friday!" and he forwards it to three friends. Then he reads the log, which is the list of steps the agent took. The last thing the agent saw was the booking form, not a confirmation, so the check never happened. To spot this, find the lap where a result proves the job is done: **no proof in the trail, no done**.
cards.simpler: Tom's agent tells him "Table booked for Friday!" and he sends it on to three friends. Then he reads the log, the list of steps the agent took. The last thing it saw was the booking form, not a confirmation, so the check never happened. To catch this, look for the lap where a result proves the job is done. **No proof in the trail, no done**.

cards.prompt: Priya's agent is on lap 4, about to ask her whether 8:30 is fine. What is the model looking at right now?

options.text: Only the last result: "8:30 is free."
The goal, plus every step and result from laps 1 to 3.
A plan it wrote at the start, which it is now following.

whyNot.a: That's the newest sticky note, not the whole stack: without the goal it wouldn't know Priya wanted 8, so it wouldn't think to ask.
whyNot.c: That's a recipe, not a loop: the agent never planned for 8pm being full. It found out on lap 2.

cards.reteach: On each lap, the model is handed everything so far, from the goal down to the newest result. That's how it knows 8:30 doesn't match the goal of 8. The newest result only makes sense next to the older ones.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
**An agent is a loop**. Picture Priya's five laps: find the page, see 8pm is full, check 8:30, ask her, book it. Each lap, the model picked one next step, software carried it out, and the result landed on the stack of sticky notes with everything before it.

It went around until a confirmation number proved the goal was met. Without that proof, only a limit you set would have stopped it.
cards.simpler: **An agent is a loop**. Think of Priya's five laps: find the page, see 8pm is full, check 8:30, ask her, book it. Each lap, the model picked one next step. Software did it. The result went on the pile of sticky notes with everything before it. Round it went until a confirmation number proved the job was done. Without that, only your limit would have stopped it.

cards.body:
On paper, draw a circle with four stops: goal, think, act, check. Walk "find a dentist open Saturday" around it, writing down what comes back on each lap. Count your laps.

Tomorrow: Tom's agent said "booked" with nothing to prove it. What stops a loop that never knows when to quit?
cards.simpler: Take a sheet of paper and draw a circle with four stops: goal, think, act, check. Now take "find a dentist open Saturday" and walk it around the circle. On each lap, write down what comes back. When you're done, **count your laps**. Tomorrow: Tom's agent said "booked" with nothing to prove it. What stops a loop that never knows when to quit?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now draw the agent loop and walk a 5-step task around it, saying what the model sees on each lap.

dubious_claims: 'Every agent runs the same loop' and 'It doesn't [write a full plan]' go too far: some agents (often called plan-and-execute agents) do write a plan up front, then revise it.
'Eleven small trips' in card 1 doesn't match the five-lap example in card 4. It's not false, but it reads like a made-up number.
The ReAct attribution to Shunyu Yao et al. is correct (2022 paper). It's listed here only because it's the chapter's one named source.
repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' teach card has no concrete image. Its teaser 'who clicks?' was already answered in card 3 ('ordinary software carries out that step'). It also isn't the chapter's last line, because the try card comes after it.
repairedFrom.fix: Rewrite the summary around Priya's five laps. End the chapter, after the try card, with a question the chapter hasn't answered, e.g. 'Tomorrow: Tom's agent said "booked" with nothing to prove it. What stops a loop that never knows when to quit?'
